title: 1 Great Number From Anthropic's IPO Prospectus and 1 Number That Disappointed
detail:
1 Great Number From Anthropic's IPO Prospectus and 1 Number That Disappointed

Bram Berkowitz, The Motley Fool

It was a long wait, but Anthropic has finally released its initial public offering prospectus as it prepares for a massive initial public offering (IPO) that could raise $100 billion at a valuation of up to $2 trillion.

While several key numbers in the prospectus had been leaked before its release, the S-1 filing confirmed the reports and provided over 400 pages of information about Anthropic's business model.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here's one great number from the IPO prospectus and one disappointing number.

Image source: Getty Images.
The good Anthropic number: 79%

I thought one of the strongest numbers in the report was 79%, representing the revenue the company generated in the third quarter ending Sept. 30 from outside its top five customers.

This shows revenue diversity, and Anthropic even said that no customer in the quarter accounted for more than 10% of the company's revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30.

Many large hyperscalers have seen significant revenue growth driven by artificial intelligence. But in some cases, it's driven by just two or three customers, which investors never like to see.

Anthropic has seen an increase in customers using its Claude family of large language models (LLMs). At the end of 2023, two customers made up 54% of total revenue.

Additionally, Anthropic disclosed that at the end of September, more than 11,900 customers had spent more than $100,000 with the company in the trailing 12 months.

For the first half of 2026, customers who spent at least $100,000 on a trailing basis accounted for 74% of the company's total revenue, so enterprise adoption is key to the company's growth.

The bad Anthropic number: 47%

While Anthropic did not provide the exact revenue it generated in the third quarter, it did provide enough information to back into the number.

In the prospectus, Anthropic states that its revenue for the three months ending Sept. 30 of this year was 86 times its revenue for the three months ending Dec. 31, 2024, which totaled $197 million. This means Anthropic generated third-quarter revenue of roughly $16.9 billion.

This means revenue grew nearly 47% from the second quarter of 2026. Now, nearly any other company that reported this kind of quarterly revenue growth would likely see their stock -- and therefore valuation -- soar.

But this is the world of artificial intelligence, where companies are trying to enter the stock market at potentially a multitrillion-dollar valuation. The 47% growth is much slower than in the second quarter, when Anthropic grew its revenue by 144% from the first quarter.

Multiple media outlets had accurately reported Anthropic's third-quarter revenue before the prospectus dropped, which led some Wall Street analysts to suggest that the company's growth may not be sufficient at its desired valuation.

"The market has moved from simply rewarding growth to asking much tougher questions about funding, cost of capital and returns on that spending," Saxo Markets chief investment strategist Charu Chanana said in a research note earlier this month.

"For Anthropic's IPO, these numbers strengthen the growth story, but valuation will still be the big debate ... A valuation above $2 trillion would be roughly 30 times annualized Q3 revenue, while investors will also have to digest the enormous infrastructure commitments required to sustain that growth."

On a more positive note, at least for the broader industry, D.A. Davidson's Gil Luria said in a research note that Anthropic's decelerating revenue growth was not due to broader AI demand but rather due to growing competition from frontier models like OpenAI and open-weight models.

Ultimately, I guess Anthropic will raise $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion in an IPO, as investors still don't want to miss out on the AI trade.

However, after going public, it could be tough sledding, similar to what Space Exploration Technologies has experienced since making its public markets debut in June.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again

In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you'd invested $5,000 then, you'd be sitting on $2,660,110 today.*

Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It's a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast.

Just after the two largest initial public offerings (IPOs) ever -- Space Exploration Technologies and SK Hynix -- Anthropic is coming through with its own IPO that's expected to topple both.

The company has been talking about going public for some time, and it filed its prospectus this past week. Will this be a great opportunity?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

What all the hype is about

Anthropic has only been around since 2021, when former OpenAI employees founded it to address disagreements they had about artificial intelligence (AI) development. They created the popular Claude AI model, and the company has become one of the most important voices in the AI community.

Image source: Getty Images.

After months of speculation about its plans, Anthropic filed a prospectus this week detailing its operations, financials, risks, and opportunities. It hasn't yet announced a price, though, and many important details were missing from the prospectus, including third-quarter performance.

What is in the prospectus, though, is fascinating, exciting, and thought-provoking. The exciting part starts with the company's recent performance. In the second quarter, revenue increased nearly 15-fold from the year-ago period to $11.6 billion. It said it has 11,900 separate customers who each pay at least $100,000, and 1,900 customers who pay at least $1 million.

The company reported $974 million in operating income in Q2, reversing what were quarterly losses. Although its net loss ballooned to $66 billion, that included a non-cash charge related to some of its private fundraising rounds. The operation is making money, but the company has other commitments eating into its profits right now.

Management has an exciting mission, and it believes that its technology can solve massive global problems and bring good to the world. It opened the prospectus by saying, "We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach, and solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort."

94 pages of risk

Notice the phrase, "if managed well." Then put that into 94 pages of risk factors, which is what's in the prospectus. There are myriad risks, starting with a danger to humanity. "Our AI models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed," is the core risk.

Home Depot (NYSE: HD) is a classic blue chip stock.

The company pioneered the big-box home improvement retail category, opening its first store in the late 1970s at a time when smaller hardware stores dominated the landscape.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

These days, Home Depot has more than 2,000 stores worldwide and earns wide profit margins and a high return on capital, a sign of its competitive advantage.

However, the stock has not been a winner in recent years. Like other stocks with exposure to the housing market, Home Depot has disappointed, as shares are actually down 11% over the last five years, badly underperforming the S&P 500 during that time, as you can see from the chart below.

HD data by YCharts

Despite the results, I still think Home Depot is worth holding for the next decade. Here are four reasons why.

1. A strong set of competitive advantages

Along with rival Lowe's, Home Depot is part of a duopoly in the home improvement retail segment.

The two companies have unmatched scale, reach, technology, and product range, which gives them significant market share in a fragmented industry.

Home Depot has differentiated itself from Lowe's in some important ways as well. Compared to Lowe's, the company is known for its focus on the professional contractor segment, and it now sees that as its primary growth opportunity. It acquired SRS Distribution, a building materials distribution company, to lean into the pro segment and grow that business.

The company has also invested heavily in omnichannel capabilities, making it easy for customers to order through its app for delivery or in-store pickup. It even offers digital project-planning apps to help consumers figure out what they need and get their projects done.

Image source: Home Depot.
2. Its industry leadership position is solid

Unlike some other retail categories, Home Depot faces little risk from disruption. It's not an easy category for a company like Amazon to gain market share in, as many of its SKUs are heavy and bulky, like lumber. Its stores also serve as distribution hubs, enabling easy pickup of e-commerce orders.

A pure-play e-commerce company wouldn't be able to compete with it, and it's hard to see another brick-and-mortar retailer expanding to match Home Depot and Lowe's.

Is Adobe the Ultimate Buy-on-the-Dip Stock?

While many companies are making a fortune from the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out, others are being actively disrupted. Adobe (NASDAQ: ADBE) is one of those companies, as its digital creation software is at risk of being replaced by AI-generated images.

However, there's a counterargument: A human touch to images is preferred in some situations, which means Adobe's software remains relevant. Adobe is also incorporating AI tools into its software to make it easier to use and more flexible.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, Adobe's stock has been a terrible performer lately because the market assumes it will be a victim of AI rather than a beneficiary. So, is it worth buying on the dip? Or are there better alternatives?

Image source: Getty Images.
Adobe's growth has barely budged

Adobe operates on a subscription platform, which makes its revenue fairly steady. Despite everyone being worried about AI disruption, Adobe has continued growing its revenue at a slow but steady pace.

ADBE Revenue (Quarterly YOY Growth) data by YCharts.

There wasn't much that changed between 2022's growth rate (prior to AI adoption) and what's being seen now. However, Adobe's stock has sold off and is down around 60% from its highest level, seen in late 2021. So, with the stock selling off heavily yet continuing to grow, the stock should be valued at a very cheap level, and that's exactly the case.

ADBE P/E Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts. P/E = price-to-earnings.

Adobe trades at just 11 times forward earnings, which clearly indicates the market is skeptical of the stock. At a price like that, Adobe's stock may seem irresistible. But is that the case? I don't think so.

The reality is that Adobe is unlikely to develop a product that enables it to deliver strong growth in the 20% to 30% range. The market will likely remain skeptical of Adobe's ability to regain market share as AI becomes more popular, so its valuation is unlikely to rebound.

Even if it does rise to market-average levels of about 20 times forward earnings, that's a single doubling, followed by market-average growth moving forward.

That's the best-case scenario, and there are many AI stocks expected to double or triple their revenue over the next few years that already trade at somewhat reasonable prices. While I don't think the outlook for Adobe is as bad as the market thinks, I also don't think it's a stock that people need to invest in. Being a hero in the stock market isn't necessary, and investors don't need to mess around with Adobe's stock when there are so many solid AI stocks available.

title: If a Recession Is Coming, History Says Utilities Aren't Safe, Just "Less Bad." Here's the Data.
detail:
If a Recession Is Coming, History Says Utilities Aren't Safe, Just "Less Bad." Here's the Data.
Todd Shriber, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 1:20 PM CDT 5 min read
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Fortunately, the strict definition of a recession, or two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, hasn't been met this year, but smart investors prepare for the worst. Preparation against economic slumps often involves embracing defensive sectors, including utilities.

Utilities join consumer staples and healthcare as traditional defensive sectors, on the basis that no matter how bad the economy gets, people will keep the lights on, continue eating, and tend to their medical needs.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Utilities stocks don't deliver big gains during recessions. Image source: Getty Images.

Still, market participants need to maintain perspective when flocking to defensive stocks for bear-market or recession protection. That's true of utilities equities, too.

Let's use the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEMKT: XLU) as the measuring stick. This exchange-traded fund (ETF) is the original dedicated utilities ETF. It turns 28 years old in December, meaning it's been around for four credible recessions: the bursting of the tech bubble (2000-02), the global financial crisis (2007-09), the 2020 economic contraction brought on by the coronavirus pandemic, and the brief "technical" recession seen in 2022.

"Less bad" is the order of the day

New investors who haven't had money on the line during bear markets or recessions should remember two things. First, outside of cash, there are no risk-free assets. Second, when opting to remain engaged with stocks during deep market pullbacks or economic calamity, don't expect big upside from defensive sectors. The most reasonable expectation is "less bad."

The SPDR ETF, which is home to the largest utilities companies by market value, proved as much during the tech bubble recession. The Nasdaq Composite hit a record on March 10, 2000, and then started a slide that lasted until Oct. 9, 2002. Over that time, the S&P 500 tumbled 42.4% while the bellwether utilities ETF slid 34.3%.

^SPX data by YCharts

On that basis, there's no denying that utilities stocks outperformed, but the group certainly wasn't "safe." It was merely "less bad."

The global financial crisis brought a sequel to that scenario. In 2008, the worst year of what was the worst recession in the U.S. since the Great Depression, the S&P 500 shed 36.8%, while the SPDR utilities ETF lost almost 29%. Over the duration of the crisis (Oct. 9, 2007, through March 9, 2009), the ETF lost 42.5% while the S&P 500 plunged nearly 56%. Clearly, the math is in favor of the utilities fund, but this is nothing to write home about.

More recent recessions

The COVID-19 recession was historically brief, and when stocks snapped out of their pandemic malaise, some speculative equities led the rebound and animal spirits were elevated, creating an environment in which defensive sectors lagged. As a result, the bellwether utilities ETF gained just 0.6% in 2020 while the S&P 500 rallied 18.4%.

Just two years later, it was a different ballgame. While the 2022 economic contraction was also considered brief, that brevity didn't protect the S&P 500 from an 18.2% drop. That year, the SPDR ETF held up well, gaining 1.4%. Arguably, that's a remarkable performance given utilities' status as bond proxies, making this a rate-sensitive sector. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates seven times in 2022.

So over the four recessions that have occurred since the State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF was born, the fund broadly did its job, even when giving it a "pass" on 2020 due to the nature of that equity market comeback. Investors just need to remember that if a historically bad recession comes to pass (hoping that won't happen), the likely best-case scenario for utilities stocks is performing less poorly than the broader market. That's it.

Is Apple a Top Tech Stock to Buy Now?

Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:50 PM CDT 3 min read

NVDA

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) has been sneakily delivering a strong 2026. It's up about 27% this year, easily outperforming the market. It's doing it without the fanfare of artificial intelligence (AI), although it has made some improvements in that area.

However, after such a great run in 2026, is it still a solid stock to buy now? I think history says it's not.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Business performance and stock performance are misaligned

Apple's business needs little introduction. Almost everyone in the U.S. has interacted with an Apple product at one time or another, and it has a strong grip on the consumer hardware space. However, this isn't typically considered a high-growth industry. Consumers only have so much money to spend on electronics and other gadgets, and Apple has saturated the market. Whether it's a phone, laptop, or watch, there's an Apple product for that. For years, Apple struggled with slow growth, but it has recently broken out above the 10% year-over-year growth mark.

AAPL Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts.

That comes after years of single-digit-to-negative growth, and it has the market excited. However, there are questions as to how long this will last. There's currently a substantial smartphone upgrade cycle underway, and once it wraps up, Apple could have a tough time keeping up with sales.

From a stock perspective, Apple's growth is underperforming its stock performance, which has pushed Apple to some valuation extremes.

Over the past decade, Apple stock breached 40 times earnings twice.

AAPL PE Ratio data by YCharts.

Each time it did so, the valuation declined by 25% to 30 times earnings or lower. That pattern looks slated to repeat itself in 2027 and could make Apple returns a bit scarce next year unless it can grow its way out of it.

However, with Wall Street analysts projecting 10% revenue growth in 2027, it's clear it won't grow substantially faster than the broader market. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) tends to grow at about a 10% pace on average. If Apple's revenue growth is at the same pace, then having nearly double the price tag doesn't make a ton of sense (the S&P 500 trades for 23.2 times earnings).

As a result, I think there are far better stocks to buy right now than Apple. The pattern is pretty clear that Apple's stock doesn't get much more expensive than this, so there will be far better times to buy in the future.

The last time the S&P 500's Shiller cyclically adjusted P/E ratio was as high as it is now, it was August 2000. The S&P 500 was sitting near an all-time high of around 1,500, in the wake of a five-plus-year bull market.

At the time, the Shiller ratio -- which gauges the 10-year inflation-adjusted valuation of the S&P 500 -- was at 41.89, down from an all-time peak of 44.19 in November 1999. What was unclear at that point was that the market was already at the beginning of a bear market that would last until November 2022.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Today, the Shiller P/E ratio is at about 41. That is the highest it has been since August 2000. Does that mean another bear market is imminent or that we are already at the start of one, as we were the last time the Shiller P/E was this high?

That's impossible to know for now. For all we know, the market could keep charging ahead into the fifth year of a bull market.

Either way, investors should apply the same discipline. They should be looking to build a diversified all-weather portfolio and take any downturn as an opportunity to buy -- not sell.

A bear market strategy

My approach in this type of market, where the large-cap index is overvalued and the economy is facing significant challenges, is to make sure my portfolio is adequately diversified.

If your portfolio has become top-heavy in tech stocks due to a four-year bull market that was largely powered by tech sector growth, you may want to make sure you rebalance it appropriately. I look for stocks that have become overvalued, meaning their valuation metrics are well outside of their typical average ranges, and I scale my positions in them back.

I also look to make sure I am adequately diversified with stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that tend to perform well when the broader market doesn't. This may include value stocks, dividend stocks, and stocks of high-quality, well-capitalized companies that generate stable, sturdy earnings in any type of market or economy.

In addition, I look for bargains, especially among tech stocks, AI stocks, or growth stocks that are trading at discounted levels, perhaps victims of broader market sell-offs. If they are market leaders with strong earnings potential and are trading below their historical P/E ratios, then they might be great options to buy on the dip.

It is important to do some additional research on why any given stock is trading at a discount, but if the company's fundamentals are strong and its advantages remain intact, then investors should be looking to buy. Because years from now, you may find that some of your best long-term investments were bought during bear markets.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Investment styles come in various shapes and sizes. Some focus on growth, others seek regular income through dividends, and others are after stability. The choice depends on many factors, including each investor's goals and preferences. But what if there were a stock that had a decent combined mix of all three of these approaches? That's not just wishful thinking, either: one company to consider along those lines is Amgen (NASDAQ:AMGN), a biotech giant.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The growth angle

Amgen has been posting strong financial results. In the second quarter, the company's revenue increased by 10% year over year -- a strong performance for a drugmaker of this size -- to $10.1 billion.

Amgen is facing the loss of patent exclusivity for denosumab, a medicine approved to treat several bone-related conditions. Sales are growing at a good clip despite that, thanks to the company's diversified portfolio.

The biotech leader had an impressive 22 products delivering at least double-digit sales growth, and 17 medicines with annualized sales of at least $1 billion in the second quarter. True, Amgen will face more patent cliffs through the end of the decade, including for Otezla and Enbrel, two immunology medicines.

But note that neither contributes much to sales growth anymore. Revenue from both medicines declined in the second quarter. Otezla is facing stiff competition, while Enbrel is succumbing to government-led price negotiations in the U.S. Their patent cliffs will accelerate sales decline. Still, Amgen has already begun moving beyond these products.

Newer therapies, most of which won't lose patent exclusivity anytime soon, are doing much of the heavy lifting in driving sales growth. The list includes Tezspire, a medicine for asthma, Tepezza, a therapy for thyroid eye disease, and Imdelltra, a cancer drug. Further, label expansions and brand-new approvals will help boost sales growth over the medium term.

For instance, Amgen recently announced positive Phase 3 clinical trial results for Imdelltra, when combined with another cancer medicine called Imfinzi, in certain patients with small-cell lung cancer. The biotech noted that the combo treatment reduced the risk of death by 58% -- an unprecedented result in this indication -- compared to Imfinzi alone.

When you wish upon a star, it seems Walt Disney (NYSE: DIS) investors had a pretty good month in October. The shares rose 6% for the month, a welcome contrast to a declining market. The stock even inched higher on Friday as the overall market tumbled.

Can Disney keep the upticks coming as we head into the holiday season? There will be a big financial update in November, as well as a high-profile theatrical release. Let's take a closer look at some of the days that Disney investors should circle for the month ahead.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Disney.
Nov. 17

Disney stock should be on the move -- one way or the other -- come Nov. 17. That's when the House of Mouse reports fourth-quarter results for fiscal 2026.

Expectations are high. Analysts see revenue rising 12% to $25.2 billion. That may not seem like a lot, but it would be Disney's first quarter of double-digit percentage revenue growth in more than three years. The news should be even better on the bottom line. Those same Wall Street pros see earnings per share soaring to $1.69, a 52% year-over-year jump.

Disney has been a standout among media stocks that have largely languished this year. The shares may have been flat over the past year, but most other leading U.S. media moguls have posted double-digit percentage declines. A strong report along with a healthy outlook can pad Disney's October gains.

Nov. 25

Disney loves releasing family-friendly fare over the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. Frozen, Toy Story, and Tangled are just some of the successful animated theatrical features it's released in late November. It has also had a few whiffs.

Hexed opens the day before Thanksgiving, giving it a five-day holiday weekend of screenings to draw families and Disney fans of all ages. The latest Disney original full-length animated feature follows an awkward teen and her demanding mother as they learn the teen's social shortcomings could be magic powers. It's fodder that's adjacent to some of Disney's bigger Thanksgiving weekend releases. I'm looking at you, Frozen and, to a lesser extent, Tangled.

It's not likely to become Disney's latest film to top $1 billion in worldwide ticket sales the way that Toy Story 5 did this summer. It doesn't have to. Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday should be the top draw of 2026. It hits theaters in December.

title: Could Rivian's Model 3 Moment Be Coming? Tesla Stock Climbed 1,364% in 3 Years.

Could Rivian's Model 3 Moment Be Coming? Tesla Stock Climbed 1,364% in 3 Years.
Daniel Miller, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 31, 2026 at 12:03 PM CDT 5 min read
RIVN
TSLA
NVDA

Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ: RIVN) investors have plenty riding on the recently launched and highly anticipated R2, and selling more vehicles would certainly be welcome. But the bigger prize is what could happen when the company gets more efficient at building them.

Fortunately, we have precedent from a fellow electric vehicle (EV) maker. Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) offers a compelling example. Its Model 3 production breakthrough helped set the stage for a much more profitable business -- and shareholders enjoyed a roller-coaster stock price ride along the way.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Could Rivian be approaching a similar turning point? There are encouraging signs, but the answer depends on more than customers wanting an R2. Let's dig in.

Rewind to Tesla's breakthrough

During the second quarter of 2018, Tesla's Model 3 gross margin turned slightly positive. Management credited lower labor hours, reduced ramp-up costs, better absorption of fixed costs, and lower material costs. Only one quarter later, Model 3 gross margin exceeded 20%, while labor hours per vehicle fell more than 30% sequentially. That happened even as Tesla shifted production toward more complex all-wheel-drive versions.

Tesla wasn't simply building more cars. It was using fewer labor hours to build each one. That doesn't necessarily mean its total labor hours declined, but it shows how a smoother production process can improve vehicle economics, requiring less labor time per vehicle.

Tesla's financial transformation quickly followed. Between the third quarter of 2018 and the third quarter of 2021, Tesla's company-wide operating margin increased from 6.1% to 14.6%. Between Sept. 28, 2018, and Sept. 30, 2021 -- the corresponding quarter-end trading dates -- its split-adjusted stock price climbed approximately 1,364%.

TSLA data by YCharts

Rivian shareholders would certainly take a helping of that, maybe even seconds. More importantly, Tesla's return reflected much more than one successful production ramp-up, and it certainly is not a forecast or prediction for Rivian. The useful lesson is how much the investment story can change when a promising vehicle becomes a profitable business.

Does Rivian have the demand?

Rivian will need ample demand to create its own Model 3 moment with its very own R2, and the early signals for R2 demand are encouraging. During its second-quarter earnings call, Rivian said reservation-to-order conversion for the roughly $58,000 R2 Launch Edition was meaningfully higher than management expected. It didn't disclose the conversion percentage, but that's a positive sign for the initial version before more affordable models of the R2 enter production.
